deep.reconstruction:
There is no computation on this page. It has two components.

(A) Main drawing. The page carries a large pencil triangle (the apex is marked with a cross or 'x'). It is filled with a pencil lattice of equilateral triangles, that is, the isometric grid with lines in the three directions 0°, 60° and 120°.
- Over the lower-left part of this grid an ink figure is drawn: bands one lattice row wide, running in the three lattice directions.
- Where bands meet, one band's edges are interrupted. This shows which band passes over the other: a planar diagram of a woven or interlaced structure (over/under crossings), drawn on the hexagonal lattice.
- The bands bend at 60°/120° and close into rhombic and hexagonal cells. In places this gives the 'isometric cube' look typical of triaxial and kagome-type weaves.
- Free band ends stick out on the left and lower-left edges (the horizontal strokes at left). This suggests a sample cut from an infinite periodic weave, not a closed knot or link.
- The neighbouring pages explain the context. The previous page is Gauss's braid of four strands a, b, c, d with complex coordinates (the 'Veränderung der Coordinaten' table) and his remarks: describe the entanglement as an aggregate of parts, count half-turns of one line about another with a fixed sense, and count sign changes + / − along each line.
- So this drawing belongs to the same 'geometria situs' / Verschlingung studies. It is an experiment in representing a multi-strand interlacing on a regular (hexagonal) grid, where crossings can be read off combinatorially.
- The ink is not fully regular: some cells are left as rhombi, others are closed as small triangles. It looks exploratory, not a finished periodic pattern.
- (Interpretation mine.) The weave is triaxial, i.e. three families of strands, one per lattice direction, crossing pairwise.

(B) Upside-down note, top left, mostly illegible. What can be read with some confidence:
- 'Die Fläche [des Vielecks/der Vielecke] …'
- '= … Kreis …' (a struck-out word)
- 'n Ecken'
- '… Seitenlänge …'
- 'Ist n = ab …'
- '… b … [Vielecke von] a Ecken'
- '3a Ecken'
- '2·3·6 …'

The most plausible content (my reconstruction, uncertain) concerns regular and star polygons with n vertices. If n = ab, the figure obtained by joining every b-th vertex splits into b separate polygons, each with a vertices. This is the standard decomposition of the star figure {n/k} into gcd(n,k) components, each with n/gcd(n,k) vertices. It may also involve the area of an inscribed regular n-gon compared with the circle.

The 'n = ab', 'a Ecken', '3a', '2·3·6' fragments may instead refer to how many polygons fit around a lattice point, or to the triangular grid of the drawing (triangle of side 3a; the 3- and 6-fold symmetry of the triangular/hexagonal lattice). No formula is legible enough to verify.
errors: No derivation to check. The drawing is not perfectly regular: some crossings are only partly inked, and band ends at the left boundary are open. It is a sketch, not a finished pattern.
The note is too fragmentary to judge its correctness.

results.what: Diagram of a woven/interlaced band structure on an equilateral-triangle (isometric) lattice, with over/under crossings shown by broken edges
results.modern_name: Triaxial weave / kagome-type weaving diagram; planar link-type diagram on the hexagonal lattice (geometria situs, knot/braid diagrams)
results.usually_credited_to: Mathematical study of weaving patterns: Grünbaum & Shephard (1980s), 'Satins and twills', 'Isonemal fabrics'. Gauss's knot/braid diagrams are discussed by Epple (1998) and Przytycki.

results.what: Fragmentary note: polygon with n = ab vertices relates to b polygons each with a vertices (probable star-polygon decomposition), possibly together with polygon area versus circle
results.modern_name: Decomposition of the star figure {n/k} into gcd(n,k) regular polygons; area of an inscribed regular n-gon
results.usually_credited_to: Star polygons: Bradwardine, Kepler; systematic treatment by Poinsot (1809)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in knots, braids and interlacings (geometria situs) is well documented, including the braid with complex coordinates on the previous page. A weaving diagram on a triangular grid fits that known programme and contains no new theorem. The upside-down note is elementary polygon material.

checkable.asserts: Joining every k-th vertex of a regular n-gon gives gcd(n,k) polygons, each with n/gcd(n,k) vertices (the 'n = ab gives b polygons of a vertices' reading).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import symbols, sin, pi, limit, oo; n=symbols('n', positive=True); limit(n/2*sin(2*pi/n), n, oo) == pi
checkable.asserts: The area of the regular n-gon inscribed in the unit circle, (n/2)·sin(2π/n), tends to the circle's area π.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import Rational; [Rational(360,1)/(180-Rational(360,m)) for m in (3,4,6)] == [6,4,3]
checkable.asserts: Only the triangle, square and hexagon fit an integer number of copies around a point (6, 4, 3), the basis of the triangular grid used in the drawing (possibly related to the '3', '6' in the note).

transcription_corrections: The upside-down note is largely illegible. Readings such as 'ursprüngl.', 'Seitenlänge' and 'Kreis' are conjectural. Better candidate readings: 'Ist n = ab …' and '… b … a Ecken' (probably about b polygons of a vertices each); '3a Ecken'; '2·3·6'.
The mark near the apex is a cross or 'x' (pencil). The drawing is ink bands over a pencil triangular lattice inside a large pencil triangle, as the transcription says.
The page number '284' is at the upper left of the page in pencil.
